introduction.text:
Fragment of 11 ll. from the middle of a multi-column tablet in Neo-Assyrian ductus, furnished with firing holes, no edges preserved. It contains the ends of ll. 148-158 of the “Poem of Creation” @i{Enūma eliš}, chapter II. As the piece is already included in the @url{/corpus/L/1/2/SB/II}{eBL Literature Corpus} edition, it will not be re-edited here, but only discussed briefly.

The fragment, excavated in 1957 in the (southern [?]) courtyard of the Nabû temple in Kalḫu, more precisely in the “upper rubbish of cutting e[astern] side of N[abû] T[emple] courtyard” (@bib{RN1696@7, 42}), was first copied by Wiseman, whose copy was later included in @i{CTN} 4. Shortly after being studied, however, the piece apparently went missing and consequently was marked as “Not traced before division” in the catalogue recording the division of finds between the British Museum and the Iraq Museum (@bib{RN1696@8 with fn. 85}). The problem seems to have lied in transposed digits in the museum number (see @i{CTN 4}: “IM 60593?”). As @bib{RN423@155 ad No. 200} states, he was informed that the fragment were to be found in a box labelled “IM 60953”, i.e. with the digits 5 and 9 in reversed order. This latter number seems to be the correct one, as Lambert was able to provide a new copy of the piece in 2013 edition of @i{Babylonian Creation Myths}.

What cannot be gleaned from either copy is the chipped-off section with a suspiciously straight break at the end of the lines. This leaves little doubt that the original tablet was in fact a multi-column one and held more than just chapter I of @i{Enūma eliš}. In this respect, it can be compared to @url{/fragmentarium/BM.98909}{BM.98909}, allegedly from Kuyunjik (note, however, the reservations concerning some of the material labelled as coming from Kuyunjik expressed by @bib{RN2170@52}). Note further the fragment @url{/fragmentarium/ND.3416}{ND.3416} from the lower edge of a tablet, containing ll. 81-91 of @i{Enūma eliš} chapter VI, which however was found in a different part of the Kalḫu citadel, namely the North-West Palace (@bib{RN1696@42}) and is thus unlikely to belong to the present piece.
